title: Word order and 'to be'
description: Build simple sentences: say what something is, where it is, and put the verb where Kannada wants it.

guide.title: The verb comes last
guide.text:
English says 'I eat rice': subject, verb, object. Kannada says 'I rice eat': subject, object, verb. The verb is always the last word of the sentence, and everything else lines up before it.

Words like 'to', 'in' and 'from' are not separate words placed before the noun; they are endings attached after it: ಶಾಲೆ (shaale) 'school', ಶಾಲೆಗೆ (shaalege) 'to school'. So 'He goes to school' is 'he school-to goes'.

The order of the pieces before the verb is fairly free, and the subject can be left out when the verb ending makes it obvious: ಹೋಗ್ತೀನಿ (hogteeni) alone means 'I am going', because -eeni can only be 'I'.

Kannada has no words for 'a' and 'the'.

examples.english: He goes to school. (he school-to goes)
I am going. / I will go.

guide.title: 'X is Y': no verb at all
guide.text:
When you say what something or someone is - a name, a job, a kind of thing - Kannada uses no verb. Just put the two side by side: ಇದು ಪುಸ್ತಕ (idu pustaka), 'this (is a) book'.

To make it negative add ಅಲ್ಲ (alla) at the end: ಇದು ಪುಸ್ತಕ ಅಲ್ಲ (idu pustaka alla), 'this is not a book'. alla never changes, whoever the subject is.

ಇದು (idu) is 'this (thing)' and ಅದು (adu) is 'that (thing)'.

guide.title: 'X is somewhere' and 'there is X': the verb iru
guide.text:
When you say where something is, or that something exists, you do need a verb: ಇರು (iru), 'to be (somewhere), to exist, to stay'. Its present forms change with the subject:

naanu iddeeni (I am), neenu iddeeya (you are, familiar), avanu iddaane (he is), avalu iddaale (she is), adu ide (it is), naavu iddeevi (we are), neevu iddeera (you are, polite or plural), avaru iddaare (they are; he or she is, respectful), avu ive (they are, of things).

The negative of all of these is the single word ಇಲ್ಲ (illa): avaru illa, 'he/she is not here'; neeru illa, 'there is no water'.

So Kannada separates two meanings of English 'is': 'is a doctor' (no verb, negative alla) and 'is at home' (iru, negative illa).

Written forms differ only slightly: iddene, iddeeya, iddaane, iddaale, ide, iddeve, iddeeri, iddaare, ive.

guide.title: Position words follow the noun
guide.text:
'On the table' is 'table's on': the noun takes the possessive ending and the position word comes after it. ಮೇಜು (meju) 'table' becomes ಮೇಜಿನ (mejina) 'of the table', then ಮೇಲೆ (mele) 'on, above'.

Useful position words: mele (on, above), kelage (under, below), olage (inside), horage (outside), hattira (near), munde (in front), hinde (behind). Several of them can also stand alone as adverbs: horage iddaare, 'they are outside'.

Short words often fuse with ide: illi + ide = illide (it is here), elli + ide = ellide (where is it?).

examples.english: The book is on the table.

phrases.note: No word for 'is' and no word for 'a'.
For a doctor you respect, say avaru daaktar.
avaru is 'they' and also the respectful 'he' or 'she'. Often shortened to aafeesalli (ಆಫೀಸಲ್ಲಿ).

phrases.english: The book is on the table.
phrases.note: Both meju and mele have a long e.
illi = here; illa = is not. Do not mix them up.
Written: tinnuttene (ತಿನ್ನುತ್ತೇನೆ). anna with dental nn is cooked rice.
makkalu is the irregular plural of magu (child).
